opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that BERT and GPT found a way to turn natural language itself into the supervision signal. Before that, most NLP progress depended on labeled datasets, and labeling is expensive, slow, and task-specific, so you could never scale it by orders of magnitude.

With BERT's masked language modeling, or GPT's next-token prediction, the text supervises itself. Any sentence on the internet becomes a training example. You hide a word or predict the next token, and the ground truth is already there. Suddenly the amount of usable training data went from millions of labeled samples to essentially the entire written record of humanity.

There's a second, subtler point. These objectives are not only scalable in data, they're also well aligned with what we want the model to learn. To predict the next word well, especially at scale, the model has to capture grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, even some understanding of the world. So the more data and compute you add, the more capability you get. That's why we later saw such clean scaling laws in language.

GPT's path in particular had a property that turned out to matter a lot: the generative objective unifies understanding and generation. Every task can be written as text in, text out. You don't need a different head or a different architecture for each task. That uniformity is what lets one model absorb more and more tasks as it grows.

Coming from computer vision, I find this contrast very instructive. In vision we tried many self-supervised methods, like contrastive learning and masked image modeling, and they worked to some degree, but we never saw the same kind of scaling behavior. I think part of the reason is that language is a human-made, highly compressed, semantically dense signal, so predicting it forces semantics. Pixels are a raw signal from nature, and predicting pixels doesn't necessarily force the model to learn high-level concepts. So the real lesson from BERT and GPT isn't just "pretrain on lots of data." It's to find a self-supervised task where scaling the data automatically scales the intelligence. Language happened to offer that very naturally.

r001.rationale: It identifies self-supervised training objectives as the core reason NLP could scale, emphasizing them over any architectural explanation.

r002.rationale: It says reliance on labeled datasets made progress expensive, slow, and task-specific, describing annotation as a scaling barrier.

r003.rationale: It explains that BERT’s masked language modeling uses text itself as supervision, so manually supplied labels are unnecessary.

r004.rationale: It connects more data and compute to greater capability, but does not state that more BERT pretraining data improves downstream task performance.

r005.rationale: It says GPT’s text-in/text-out objective unifies tasks, but does not identify in-context modeling as the means.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key is that they found a way to turn the unlimited supply of raw text into a useful training signal, and the amount of signal kept growing with the amount of data and compute you threw at it.

Before BERT and GPT, the strongest NLP results came from supervised tasks, and supervised data is expensive. You can label a few hundred thousand sentences, maybe a few million, but you cannot label the internet. So every model hit a ceiling set by how much annotation you could afford. Pretraining on word vectors like word2vec helped a bit, but the representation was shallow, one vector per word, and the downstream model still had to learn almost everything from the small labeled set.

What BERT and GPT did was make the task itself self-supervised. Predict the next token, or predict the masked token. The labels come for free from the text. That sounds trivial, but it changes the economics completely. The bottleneck shifts from human labeling to compute, and compute is something you can scale by writing a cheque.

The second ingredient is the Transformer. Earlier recurrent models did not scale well in depth or sequence length, and they were hard to parallelize. The Transformer is almost embarrassingly parallel, it is friendly to GPUs, and empirically it keeps improving when you make it bigger. So you have a cheap objective and an architecture that absorbs scale without saturating. Put those two together and you get a very clean loop: more data, more parameters, more compute, better model. Researchers could follow that loop for years without needing a new idea each step.

I would also add that the pretrain-then-finetune recipe made the field converge. Instead of every task having its own architecture, everyone started from the same backbone, which meant improvements to the backbone transferred to everything. In computer vision we had that with ImageNet pretraining much earlier, and I think BERT and GPT were essentially NLP finding its ImageNet moment, except with an objective that did not depend on labels at all. That is why it opened a road rather than just a single result.

r001.rationale: The response makes self-supervised training objectives the key driver, then presents the Transformer as a second ingredient.

r002.rationale: It says supervised data is expensive to label and that annotation limits how much training data is available.

r003.rationale: It explains that BERT predicts masked tokens and gets labels directly from text, without manual annotation.

r004.rationale: It says more data and compute improve models generally, but does not clearly connect more BERT masked-token pretraining data to improved downstream task performance.

r005.rationale: It describes shared pretraining and fine-tuning across tasks, but does not identify in-context modeling as unifying downstream tasks for GPT.

astra-6.text:
I think the key was that they turned the enormous amount of text already available into training data, without requiring people to label it manually. BERT learns by predicting masked words, and GPT learns by predicting the next token. Those objectives are simple, but they push a model to learn patterns that are useful across many language tasks.

That gave researchers a common foundation: pretrain a general model, then adapt it to particular applications, instead of building a separate system for every task. And with the Transformer architecture, training could make effective use of large-scale computation. So there was a clear path forward—more data, larger models, and more compute could improve the same basic approach. To me, that combination of self-supervision, reusable representations, and scalable training was the important breakthrough.

r001.rationale: The response calls using available text without manual labels “the key” and emphasizes self-supervision and training scalability, while describing the Transformer as helpful for computation.

r002.rationale: It identifies manual labeling as something that would otherwise be required, and explains that avoiding it lets existing text become training data.

r003.rationale: It says BERT predicts masked words and connects that objective to learning from available text without manually supplied labels.

r004.rationale: It says more data can improve the general approach, but does not specifically state that more BERT cloze-pretraining data improves downstream task performance.

r005.rationale: It describes pretraining followed by adaptation to applications, but does not identify in-context modeling as unifying downstream tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key was that they turned raw text into a training signal. You no longer needed people to label every example for every task. BERT learned by predicting masked words, and GPT learned by predicting the next token, so both could benefit from enormous amounts of unlabeled text.

That gave the field a repeatable path: train a general model on more data with more compute, then adapt it to particular tasks. The Transformer architecture made that training practical at scale. So instead of designing a separate system for each language problem, researchers could improve a shared foundation and carry those improvements across many tasks.

r001.rationale: It presents learning from raw text through training objectives as the key to scalability, while describing the Transformer as making training practical at scale.

r002.rationale: It says researchers no longer needed people to label every example for every task, identifying manual annotation as a scaling obstacle.

r003.rationale: It explains that BERT predicts masked words and that unlabeled text can supply the training signal without task-specific manual labels.

r004.rationale: It says both models benefit from abundant unlabeled text and describes adapting a general model to tasks, but does not clearly state that more BERT cloze-pretraining data improves downstream task performance.

r005.rationale: It mentions GPT’s next-token prediction and adapting models to tasks, but does not identify in-context modeling as the mechanism unifying downstream tasks.
